guide.title: Terminal block wire size chart: AWG to mm² for panel wiring
guide.description: Convert AWG to mm² for terminal blocks, see which nominal block size fits each wire, and learn why ferrules change the maximum conductor size
keyTakeaways: AWG and mm² sizes don't line up exactly, so use the nearest metric size the datasheet lists
A block's nominal size is a rating, not the largest wire it accepts
Ferrules reduce the largest conductor a clamp will take, so check the ferruled range

body.text: Terminal block datasheets list conductor sizes in square millimetres (mm²), while North American drawings usually call for AWG. The table below converts the common panel sizes and shows the metric size you will normally see on a terminal block datasheet for each AWG wire.
What the nominal size on a terminal block means

Most DIN-rail terminal blocks are named after their nominal cross-section, such as a 2.5 or a 4. That number is the rated conductor size the block is tested with. It is not the largest wire the block accepts: a 2.5 mm² block often takes solid conductors up to 4 mm², and smaller conductors down to around 0.2 mm². The full range is in the datasheet.

body.caption: Phoenix Contact PT 2,5 and UT 4: the number in the name is the nominal cross-section in mm².

body.text: Datasheets usually give separate ranges for solid wire, stranded wire, and stranded wire with a ferrule. AWG ranges are listed separately again, because they come from UL testing rather than IEC testing. Always check the line that matches the conductor you will actually use.

A ferrule adds a metal sleeve, and insulated ferrules add a plastic collar. Both make the conductor bigger at the clamp, so the largest ferruled conductor a block accepts is often one size smaller than the largest bare conductor. If your shop standard calls for ferrules on every stranded wire, size the block from the ferruled range.
Picking a block from the wire size

items: Find the AWG on the drawing and convert it with the chart above
Choose a block whose range covers that size for your conductor type, with or without ferrules
Check the current rating against the circuit, not just the wire size
Use the same block size for neighbouring circuits where you can, so jumpers and end plates match

body.caption: Smaller blocks save rail space; double-level blocks save even more for control wiring.

body.title: Sourcing tip
body.text: List the wire size and whether you use ferrules when you order. Two blocks with the same nominal size can have different ranges, and that detail is what decides whether a substitute will fit.

Control circuits in North American panels are commonly wired in 16 or 18 AWG, which sit comfortably in 1.5 mm² and 2.5 mm² blocks. Power distribution often moves to 14, 12 or 10 AWG, which calls for 4 mm² to 6 mm² blocks or larger. Grounding conductors follow the same sizing, using green-yellow PE blocks of the matching size.

faqs.q: Is 14 AWG the same as 2.5 mm²?
faqs.a: Not exactly. 14 AWG is about 2.08 mm². It is usually terminated in a 2.5 mm² terminal block, because 2.5 mm² is the nearest standard metric size and covers 14 AWG in its range.

faqs.q: Can I put two wires in one terminal block clamp?
faqs.a: Only if the datasheet allows it. Many blocks list a two-conductor range, often requiring twin ferrules. Otherwise use a block with more connection points or a jumper to a second block.

faqs.q: Why does the datasheet list a different AWG range than the mm² range?
faqs.a: AWG ranges come from UL testing and mm² ranges from IEC testing. The two standards test differently, so the ranges don't always convert exactly. Use the range that matches the approval your panel needs.
